The China Shock and Manufacturing Employment in the United States

Model report — Diversity in a Globalized World

Author

Example team: Name 1, Name 2, Name 3

Published

September 9, 2026

Show Code 
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# One file. It holds the map and the data together.
zones <- st_read("data/china_shock/china_shock.gpkg", quiet = TRUE)

Research question

Did the parts of the United States most exposed to Chinese imports lose more manufacturing jobs?

Motivation

Between 1991 and 2007 China went from a minor exporter to the largest manufacturing exporter in the world. That change did not arrive evenly. Some places made furniture, textiles and toys — exactly what China began to export. Others made things China did not export.

If globalization spreads its costs unevenly, we should be able to see it on a map.

Data

We use the replication data from Autor, Dorn and Hanson (2013), The China Syndrome, published in the American Economic Review.

One observation = one commuting zone: a local labour market, defined as a group of counties that people travel between for work. The continental US has 722.

Show Code 
zones |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(exposure, manuf_change, manuf_1990) |>
  summary()
    exposure          manuf_change        manuf_1990     
 Min.   : 0.000002   Min.   :-23.4701   Min.   : 0.6904  
 1st Qu.: 0.924520   1st Qu.: -4.4682   1st Qu.:12.0067  
 Median : 2.566071   Median : -2.1465   Median :21.3734  
 Mean   : 3.425984   Mean   : -2.5557   Mean   :22.1312  
 3rd Qu.: 4.518994   3rd Qu.: -0.3045   3rd Qu.:30.2650  
 Max.   :49.004984   Max.   :  6.5501   Max.   :61.8197
Variable What it measures
exposure Chinese imports per worker, 1990–2007 (USD)
manuf_change Change in the % of jobs in manufacturing, 1990–2007
manuf_1990 % of jobs in manufacturing in 1990
region Census region

Exposure is not measured by what a zone imported. It is measured by what the zone produced before China grew. A town full of furniture factories counts as highly exposed even if it never imported anything.

Map 1 — Where did the shock land?

Show Code 
ggplot(zones) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = exposure), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1, trans = "sqrt",
                       name = "USD per\nworker") +
  labs(title = "Exposure to Chinese imports, 1990–2007") +
  theme_void()

The shock concentrates in the southeast — North Carolina and Tennessee, furniture and textiles — and along the Indiana–Ohio industrial corridor. The agricultural plains barely register.

NoteWhy trans = "sqrt"

Exposure runs from near 0 to 49 USD, but the median is 2.6. On a linear scale almost the whole map is one colour and three zones are black. The square root lets you see variation where most of the cases actually are.

Map 2 — Where were the jobs lost?

Show Code 
ggplot(zones) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = manuf_change), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis",
                       name = "Change in %\nmanufacturing\nemployment") +
  labs(title = "Change in manufacturing employment, 1990–2007") +
  theme_void()

The pattern resembles Map 1 but is not identical. That difference is the interesting part: if the two maps matched perfectly, exposure would explain everything.

Map 3 — Who was vulnerable beforehand?

Show Code 
ggplot(zones) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = manuf_1990), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "mako", direction = -1,
                       name = "% jobs in\nmanufacturing\n1990") +
  labs(title = "Dependence on manufacturing before the shock (1990)") +
  theme_void()

A zone loses manufacturing jobs if (a) the shock reached it and (b) it had manufacturing to lose. The three maps together separate those two things.

Simple graph — The main relationship

Show Code 
ggplot(zones, aes(x = exposure, y = manuf_change)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "#0f6f96") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#b44527") +
  labs(title = "More exposure, larger fall in manufacturing employment",
       x = "Exposure to Chinese imports (USD per worker)",
       y = "Change in % manufacturing employment") +
  theme_minimal()
Show Code 
cor(zones$exposure, zones$manuf_change, use = "complete.obs") |> round(3)
[1] -0.393

The correlation is −0.39: negative and clear. Each dot is one commuting zone.

Complex graph — What the simple one hides

The graph above mixes two things together. Here we split by region and add prior manufacturing dependence as colour:

Show Code 
ggplot(zones, aes(x = exposure, y = manuf_change)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = manuf_1990), alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#b44527", linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "mako", direction = -1,
                        name = "% manufacturing\nin 1990") +
  facet_wrap(~ region) +
  labs(title = "The same relationship, split by region",
       subtitle = "Colour shows how much manufacturing the zone had before the shock",
       x = "Exposure to Chinese imports (USD per worker)",
       y = "Change in % manufacturing employment") +
  theme_minimal()

What this adds: the negative slope appears in all four regions, so it is not an artefact of one part of the country. And the darker points — zones with more manufacturing in 1990 — sit lower: exposure hurts more where there was more to lose.

Interpretation

  1. The shock was geographically uneven. It did not arrive in “the United States”. It arrived in the textile southeast and the industrial midwest.

  2. More exposure goes with larger manufacturing losses (r = −0.39), and the relationship holds inside every region.

  3. Prior vulnerability matters. The damage depends on the shock and on how much manufacturing was there to begin with.

What the map shows that a table cannot: exposure and job loss concentrate in the same regions, but not perfectly. A table sorted by exposure would show the correlation. Only the map shows that the shock has a shape — the southeast and the midwest — and that this shape is why a national phenomenon was experienced as a regional collapse.

Limitations

  • Correlation, not causation. Something else could have caused both. Autor, Dorn and Hanson instrument exposure using Chinese imports to other rich countries; we do not.
  • A zone is not a person. A zone losing jobs does not tell us what happened to any individual worker.
  • Manufacturing only. We do not measure whether those jobs reappeared in other sectors.
  • Approximate geography. The map uses 2015 counties with a 1990 crosswalk; some boundaries changed in between.

Use of AI

Task AI? What we asked How we checked it
geom_sf error Yes Explain a projection error Compared against the sf documentation and re-ran
Choosing a colour scale Yes Options for skewed data Tried linear and sqrt; we chose
Interpretation No — —
Writing Yes Check clarity of two paragraphs Reviewed every change

Example prompt:

“I have an sf object called zones with one row per commuting zone. exposure is numeric and heavily right-skewed. Using ggplot2, make a choropleth map and explain each line.”

What we changed afterwards: it suggested scale_fill_gradient() on a linear scale. When we looked at the result, nearly the whole map was one colour. We switched to viridis with trans = "sqrt".

Reference

Autor, D. H., Dorn, D., & Hanson, G. H. (2013). The China Syndrome: Local Labor Market Effects of Import Competition in the United States. American Economic Review, 103(6), 2121–2168.
